plan: [ This is strategically equivalent to a second-price auction: winner pays the second-highest sealed bid. With independent private values, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy. Underbidding risks losing when profitable; overbidding risks winning at a price above value if the second-highest bid exceeds your value. Since there is only 1 round, no learning advantage exists. To maximize expected profit, set the sealed bid equal to my value so I stay in until the price reaches $31 and win precisely when it’s profitable. ]

[ This is strategically equivalent to a sealed-bid second-price auction, since the winner pays the second-highest sealed bid (the clock price when the second-to-last exits). The dominant strategy is to bid my true value. Overbidding risks paying above my value if the second-highest lies between my value and my bid; underbidding risks losing profitable wins. With no history and one round, there’s no reason to deviate. I will bid exactly my value, 22, to maximize expected profit. I will win when both rivals’ bids are below 22 and pay the second-highest among them. ]

[ This mechanism is effectively a second-price auction since the winner pays the second-highest sealed bid via the exit clock. In such auctions, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy: it maximizes expected profit regardless of others’ actions. Underbidding risks losing when price is below your value; overbidding risks winning at a price above your value if the second-highest bid exceeds your value. There’s only 1 round and no history to exploit, so truthtelling is optimal. With value = 40, bid 40 to ensure you win whenever it’s profitable and never pay more than your value. ]
